extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students in introductory proof-based mathematics (learning proof techniques)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for writing and evaluating elementary mathematical proofs (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, existence/uniqueness, if-and-only-if, and elementary set proofs) aimed at beginning proof-based courses. Covers how to set up proofs, when to use each technique, and common structural advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction for universal statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof by contradiction often works well in proving statements of the form ∀x, P(x). The proof setup assumes ¬(∀x, P(x)) which is equivalent to ∃x, ¬P(x), giving a specific x for which ¬P(x) is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this when the negation produces a concrete counterexample (a specific x) that you can exploit to derive a contradiction. Example: assume there exists x in [0, π/2] with sin x + cos x < 1 and derive impossibility. This gives a clear path to contradict known properties of that x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving a conditional statement by contradiction (outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'If P, then Q' by contradiction, assume the negation of the implication: equivalently assume P and ¬Q, and derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin the proof with the line 'Suppose P and ¬Q.' Then proceed until you deduce both C and ¬C (or otherwise impossible statement). Example: for 'if a^2 is even then a is even' start 'suppose a^2 is even and a is not even' which yields contradiction. This is a standard template; be explicit about the assumed P and ¬Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine proof techniques when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: In more complex proofs several proof techniques may be combined within a single proof (e.g., overall direct proof that contains a proof by contradiction for a subclaim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to have 'proofs inside of proofs.' If the truth of an intermediate statement R together with P implies Q, prove R using whichever method is appropriate (direct/contrapositive/contradiction), then continue the outer proof. Keep the structure clear so the reader sees which subproof serves which role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct/contrapositive over contradiction when simpler
rubrics_metrics.description: Although proof by contradiction is powerful, it's best to use it only when direct and contrapositive approaches do not seem to work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proof by contradiction can often hide a simpler contrapositive proof. If part of a contradiction proof effectively assumes ¬Q and deduces ¬P, prefer writing the contrapositive proof directly. This yields clearer and more efficient proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for proving 'P if and only if Q'
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a biconditional 'P if and only if Q', prove both conditional statements: P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ P (each may use direct, contrapositive or contradiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin a new paragraph for the second direction; it's good to start that paragraph with the word 'Conversely' and remind the reader which implication is being proved. Use any technique appropriate for each direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving multiple statements are equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a list of statements are equivalent, it suffices to prove conditional implications in a pattern (often circular) so that each statement implies another and the chain returns to the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A circular chain (a⇒b⇒c⇒...⇒a) minimizes the number of implications to prove. Other patterns (mixing ⇐⇒ and ⇒) also work. Prove each conditional by whichever method (direct/contrapositive/contradiction) is convenient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence proofs — provide an example
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove ∃x, R(x) is true, give a specific example x for which R(x) holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Display and verify the example. The amount of verification needed depends on the example; do not merely assert it without demonstration (e.g., show 1729 = 1^3 + 12^3 = 9^3 + 10^3). WARNING: an example suffices for existence but does not prove conditional statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence inside a conditional (construct explicit witness depending on assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: For conditional statements that assert existence (e.g., if a,b in Z then ∃k,ℓ such that ...), assume the hypothesis and then produce integers (which may depend on the hypotheses) that satisfy the existential claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the existential as the goal within a direct proof: under the assumption produce explicit witnesses and verify they satisfy the required relation (example: proof that gcd(a,b)=ak+ bℓ constructs the minimal positive element of a certain set and shows it equals gcd).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness proofs — existence plus uniqueness argument
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'there is a unique x for which P(x)', first produce an x = d for which P(d) holds, then show any other candidate must equal d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common pattern: assume d' also has the property; show d' ≤ d and d ≤ d' (or show difference is zero), hence d' = d. Example: uniqueness of the natural number d such that multiples of d equal set {ax+by}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive versus non-constructive existence proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive proofs give an explicit example; non-constructive proofs show existence without constructing a specific example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be able to recognize both. Non-constructive example: arguing that either √2^√2 is irrational (giving irrational^irrational rational) or otherwise (a different construction) yields the existence of irrational x,y with x^y rational, without identifying which case holds. Constructive proof exhibits explicit x,y and verifies they work; if using non-constructive method, it's acceptable but note it doesn't identify the witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to show a ∈ {x : P(x)} (set-builder element proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A = {x : P(x)}, to show a ∈ A show that P(a) is true. If A = {x ∈ S : P(x)}, show a ∈ S and P(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand set-builder notation and explicitly verify the defining predicate(s). Provide examples to demonstrate the method. This is the basic criterion for membership proofs and should be applied directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to prove A ⊆ B (direct, contrapositive, or contradiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A ⊆ B means if a ∈ A then a ∈ B. Prove this conditional directly by assuming a ∈ A and deducing a ∈ B, or contrapositive by assuming a ∉ B and deducing a ∉ A; you may also use contradiction by assuming a ∈ A and a ∉ B and deriving a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct approach is usually the most straightforward; use contrapositive when more expedient. Present the assumed element a and clearly manipulate definitions (e.g., divisibility) to conclude membership. Examples in the text illustrate proving subset relations among divisibility-based sets and intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural clarity and reader orientation in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proof contains multiple parts or changes technique (e.g., proving two directions, or embedding subproofs), structure the proof with paragraphs and explicit transition words ('Conversely', 'To finish', etc.) reminding the reader of the current goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin new paragraphs for distinct parts (such as the second direction in an iff proof). Clearly state assumptions at the start (e.g., 'Suppose a ∈ A' or 'Suppose P and ¬Q') and conclude statements explicitly (e.g., 'Thus A ⊆ B'). This helps readers follow multi-step and nested arguments.
